body:
First, I think this is an important problem to solve, and something that severely cripples custom elements today. However, I have many reservations about this proposed solution.

Framing it these behaviors around a "submit button" all-or-nothing black box **significantly limits their utility**. I understand the intent to make simple things easy, but we usually want to make complex things possible _first_, unless use cases are very strongly concentrated around a few simple things, so the friction this would add to the simple cases is not worth it. 

I don't think that's the case here *at all*. In fact, I'd argue that submit buttons are a tiny subset of use cases for some of these behaviors:
1. Nearly every UI widget needs focusability. Once you have focusability, `:focus`, `:focus-visible` should Just Work™ without any additional wiring.
2. Literally every custom form element would benefit from access to `:default`, `:disabled`/`:enabled` (and also things like `:in-range`, `:out-of-range`, `:indeterminate`, `:checked`, etc). Not sure why `:hover` and `:active` are in that list of pseudo-classes, as these already work on any element.

I think adding these as button-shaped black boxes *before* we have any other way to achieve them individually is quite dangerous, as it can lead to workarounds where custom elements have to claim to be something they are not, simply to get focusability or certain pseudo-classes.

Once you remove these two "big ticket" items above, what remains is:
- ARIA (already covered via `ElementInternals.role` and friends)
- Implicit submission and activation, which are trivial for authors to implement

So I would suggest focusing efforts on 1 and 2 **separately**, which are truly very pressing needs. Once these are possible, we can see if additional API surface to make simple things easy is warranted, _what_ these simple things are, and what options the platform provides for making them easy at the time. 

Why not work on both in parallel? Because the API design of packaging up things that are *already* possible is quite different from the API design of packaging things up that are *not* otherwise possible. For example, the former could even be done with UA-provided traits, and there is [active TC39 work around traits](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-first-class-protocols) that may become relevant if it advances by then (I got involved in it exactly because there are so many WC needs that would benefit).

-----

Additionally, as I mentioned in the call, we cannot design a good solution without a concrete, complete list of needs. A lot of API design is around connecting the dots, and you can't do that well if some dots are missing!

**What are the low-level native platform behaviors we want to make available?** The list in the OP is not complete. Other examples that were mentioned:
- Triggering popovers via `popovertargetaction`
- Triggering commands via `command` and `commandfor`
- Being labelable (see also #11584)
- Arrow key navigation (see #11752)
- Inherent draggability (see #11752)

Which others are there?

Per the whatwg meeting my general pieces of feedback to this proposal are:

1. This looks like a really nice refinement on the original proposal. Moving toward a shape of "attaching objects as behaviours" feels like there is a lot more scope for design, including for downstream tooling like type systems and linters.
2. I would like to see more of a design of how userland script might be able to integrate with this. It will definitely be asked for (custom element cooperative behaviours are very common in frameworks). It might also help "explain" the feature to developers, for example rather than `HTMLSubmitButtonBehavior` being simply a magical sentinel value, a developer might reason about how they could implement themselves, which will also be useful when adding new behaviours - as they will be possible to polyfill. I don't think the initial ship needs to necessarily immediately ship with a userland implementation but we should definitely have a design/proposal so that we can understand how to follow up with this. The current proposal mentions this but doesn't explore it further and that to me is a gap.
3. I have some minor grievances with particulars of the API; `.attachInternals({ behaviours: [...] })` as an array seems problematic because it becomes a can of worms, for e.g. what does `.attachInternals({ behaviours: [HTMLSubmitButtonBehavior, HTMLSubmitButtonBehavior] })` do?
4. Similar to the problems with an array during construction, it also seems unfortunate to have an array _after_ construction, especially if it's mutable - I can foresee unpleasant userland code like `for (const behavior of behaviors) if (behavior instanceof HTMLSubmitButtonBehavior)` to try to get to the one desired behavior, or _worse_ developers being surprised that `behaviors[0]` _isn't_ their desired behavior.
5. A tiny nit: `attachInternals({behaviors})` vs IDL `internals.beahviorList` is inconsistent, we should pick one name, IMO.

@justinfagnani hey, those open questions and alternatives are mainly about the plain JS API shape possibilities, but don't mention the type checking, intellisense, and IDE possibilities for a well-typed experience. That's what I'm trying to address.

A well-typed experience means if I write a class definition that uses certain behaviors, my IDE will list only the relevant APIs (for example in an autocomplete popup) for those behaviors as non-nullable members, and will not flood my experience with a bunch of properties that don't exist that I'm not using. It means I will know exactly for sure which APIs I can work with, without noise, without having to write nullish guards or non-null assertions.

---

The class-factory mixin approach does offer a well-typed solution, while some of the other approaches don't.

So above, I'm describing three alternatives as they relate to having a well-typed experience (including class-factory mixins).
The proposal doesn't change the public API of elements, so there's no type-checking, etc., impact.

If behaviors will ever add new properties anywhere (on the element, or some other property object like ElementInternals), now or in the future, then the chosen approach will either

1. expose them all into a single bag (or multiple bags) of nullable properties for an unknown set of applied behaviors,
2. or make the behaviors statically analyzable so that we can have selective non-nullable properties based on which behaviors static analysis tools like TypeScript have detected are in use

It is inevitable that this API will go down one of these two paths. 100%

As an example, the OP describes one possibility such as 

```js
this._internals.behaviors.htmlSubmitButton.formAction = '/custom';
```

where for example the object `this._internals.behaviors` will need to contain a bag of nullable properties for every behavior that could possibly exist because it isn't statically analyzable: TypeScript has no mechanism to dynamically add or remove property definitions from a single object based on runtime function calls that are located elsewhere.

So what I'm expressing is that a statically analyzable API design would be nicer, if doable.

In fact that's why I've dropped my usage of `element-behaviors` and `custom-attributes`, because TypeScript has no machinery to statically analyze those so the definition for an element has to necessarily contain every possible property of every possible custom attribute even if none are being used, which makes the IDE experience very bad. But hey, maybe if they became native, TS would add such machinery (including for JSX?).

I've moved onto behaviors-as-child-elements (that don't render any content) in that scenario, because elements are one thing that TypeScript does have static machinery for (f.e. JSX.IntrinsicElements).

Class-factory mixins naturally fit statically into that machinery.

@anaskim 
> Thank you for the feedback! I've updated the explainer and the original description of this issue.
> 
> [@LeaVerou](https://github.com/LeaVerou), I agree that focusability and pseudo-class access are pressing needs that would benefit many use cases beyond submit buttons. However, I don't think we need to choose between primitive behaviors and bundled behaviors. Both can advance in parallel. [...] Starting with a focused behavior lets us validate the overall pattern (conflict resolution strategies, lifecycle semantics, etc.) before expanding to more capabilities.

I’ve addressed this in my earlier comment:

> Why not work on both in parallel? Because the API design of packaging up things that are _already_ possible is quite different from the API design of packaging things up that are _not_ otherwise possible. 

Whether you ship low-level first or high-level first is a fundamental architectural decision, not "hey why don't we also add another feature". 

Typically, the pain of things not being possible exceeds the pain of things not being easy, so _usually_ you want to err on the side of addressing the former first. Addressing the most pressing pain points (things not being possible) buys you more time to make them easy, which typically leads to better high-level solutions.

There _are_ valid cases where you want to ship high-level APIs first, and we do it often. Some of the considerations are:
- How variable are use cases? Could a high-level solution satisfy 80% of them? ([Pareto principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle))
- How confident are we that we know the landscape of use cases well? Would shipping low-level primitives get us more data?
- How painful would the high-level API be to emulate once users have the low-level APIs?
- Is the high-level API easier for UAs to implement?
- Does shipping the high-level API provide additional benefits over the union of low-level APIs? (e.g. privacy, not having to update code when new browser versions are out, etc)
- Does shipping the high-level API first back you into a corner when it comes to future improvements, or can the low-level improvements simply be retrofitted in to explain it?

It was answering these questions that make me think that shipping the low-level API first is a better path forwards, not some intrinsic eagerness for scope creep.

More specifically:
- I’m very unconvinced that submit buttons are a majority use case, let alone the top one, and I’m concerned that the current API has [overfit](https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/overfitting-and-the-problem-with-use-cases-337d9f4bf4d7) to this one use case. It’s ok to focus an MVP around one use case, but you need to have a plan for how to develop it later. What other behaviors might we need to add? How do we customize them? What is the mental model around what becomes a behavior and what becomes an `ElementInternals` setting?
- I’m unconvinced that if we had all the low-level pieces in place, the high-level API would be significantly more painful to emulate, but with no comprehensive list of what the low-level behaviors are exactly this is hard to answer.
- A potential benefit of the high-level approach would be that authors don't need to be aware of what the low-level behaviors are, so web components get them at the same speed as native elements. That would be very compelling, but given that these behaviors do not add API surface, authors already need to be aware of them so they can add the glue code.

Additionally, I have several architectural concerns around this approach:
- Currently, this provides **neither the efficiency of a high-level feature (since any API surface needs manual glue code), nor the flexibility of a low-level one**. Once the low-level pieces are in place, behaviors could ship as a high-level primitive that *both* packages the behavior AND provides API surface, using whatever mechanisms we have at the time for that.
- It is introducing a mechanism that is essentially inheritance or traits without using language primitives for any of these
- The properties within each behavior actively conflict with existing ElementInternals primitives, complicating the mental model. 
- No comprehensive list of low-level behaviors that this is abstracting has been provided, despite several requests for one. So we're trying to validate an abstraction without a clear picture of what it’s abstracting. It is even more worrying if no such list exists, meaning the abstraction itself was designed without full awareness of what behaviors it would pull in.
- It’s okay to design a general purpose API and ship a much smaller subset to start with. But you still need at least a rough idea of what the larger subset would look like. So far, any attempt to generalize this beyond buttons has failed to get consensus.

> The bundled approach (like `HTMLSubmitButtonBehavior`) addresses a concrete use case that frameworks are actively working around today (as documented in the [user research section](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md?rgh-link-date=2026-02-20T19%3A13%3A45.000Z#user-research) with Shoelace, Material Web, etc.). 

For context, the user research section consists of:
1. Links to past discussions about *much* broader sets of use cases to which this seems to have no natural evolution towards. I was there at both TPAC discussions listed (although oddly I'm not listed as a participant in the first one (but I’m minuted)) and co-chaired the second one. The needs that motivate custom attributes are fundamentally different to the needs motivating these element behaviors. One is about reusing native elements (or even existing web components) so we don't have to recreate our own, this one about making it easier to recreate them. But the core motivation behind custom attributes is not around the difficulty of re-creating custom elements, but around composability and compatibility.
2. Links to past discussions about exactly the types of low-level features I was saying the platform needs: form submission, popover invocation, custom elements as forms, etc.
3. This section around examples from existing components (this is the entirety of it):

> 3. Real-world use cases from frameworks that work around these limitations:
> 
>    - [Shoelace](https://github.com/shoelace-style/shoelace/blob/next/src/components/button/button.component.ts#L180): Uses `ElementInternals` but still requires manual wiring to intercept the click event on its internal shadow button (as shown below) and can't support implicit submission ("Enter to submit").
> 
>    ```javascript
>    // button.component.ts
>    handleClick(event) {
>      if (this.type === 'submit') {
>        this._internals.form.requestSubmit(this);
>      }
>    }
>    ```
> 
>    - [Material Web](https://github.com/material-components/material-web/blob/main/button/internal/button.ts): Renders a `<button>` inside the Shadow DOM for accessibility/clicks. They created a [dedicated class](https://github.com/material-components/material-web/blob/main/internal/controller/form-submitter.ts) to handle form submission and intercept the click event to call `form.requestSubmit(this)`.
> 
>    - Older method (used by earlier design systems): To enable implicit submission, the component injects a hidden `<button type="submit">` into its own light DOM. This approach breaks encapsulation, risks unintended layout effects by participating in the parent’s flow or the surrounding container, and can pollute the accessibility tree.
> 
>    ```html
>    <ds-button>
>      #shadow-root
>      <button>Click Me</button>
>      <button type="submit" style="display: none;"></button> 
>    </ds-button>
>    ```

This demonstrates a need, yes. But nobody questioned that the need exists! The qualms were around where it stands relative to similar needs and whether this is the right API shape and the right abstraction level at this point in time. Anecdotally, having worked on one of these frameworks (Web Awesome, neé Shoelace), I recall numerous needs around extending or wrapping native elements that were more pressing (e.g. extending `<input>`).

-----

Thinking some more, if the main pressing use case is buttons, what if we could enable exactly that, but in a way that works with existing platform primitives?
Reading the explainer:
> Use customized built-ins (is/extends syntax), which have [Shadow DOM limitations](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/attachShadow#elements_you_can_attach_a_shadow_to) and [can't use the ElementInternals API](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5166).

I wonder if we could special-case `HTMLButtonElement` so that subclassing could work just for that:
```js
class CustomSubmitButton extends HTMLButtonElement {
	constructor () {
		super();
		super.type = "submit";
	}
}

customElements.define("custom-submit-button", CustomSubmitButton);
```

No `is`, just purely JS/behavior inheritance.

Pros:
- It gets API surface, so it's truly high-level
- Inheritance chain that actually makes sense and uses existing language primitives
- There is no reason Shadow DOM wouldn't work. It's a custom element, and buttons don’t typically have a shadow DOM in any UA I’ve tested, so conflicts shouldn't be a problem.
- There is no reason `ElementInternals` wouldn’t work. The linked issue is about the presence of an `is` attribute, which would not exist in this case.

Sure, there may be use cases that need to pull in multiple behaviors, but we could explore that separately (e.g. via individual `ElementInternals` settings). So far behaviors have centered around buttons, which it seems something like this could address just fine.

Thanks for the continued discussion—this feedback is really helpful for shaping the proposal.

@trusktr
> As for named behaviors, let's imagine for example that in the future an app has 100 or more behaviors (whether custom or built-in). Does this mean all the named behaviors would need to be registered onto an interface (similar to TypeScript's HTMLElementTagNameNap orJSX.IntrinsicElements) and thus internals.behaviors would have 100 or more nullable keys?

This is one reason the [instantiated behaviors pattern](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#alternative-1-use-behaviors-everywhere-instantiated-behaviors) seems attractive. For platform behaviors, the set would likely stay small, so named access via `internals.behaviors.htmlSubmitButton` seems manageable there. For developer-defined behaviors at scale, I'm inclined to think named registration shouldn't be required as developers would use the instantiated pattern and access behaviors via their own private fields.

---

@LeaVerou
One clarification on framing: the proposal is about **enabling custom elements to participate in form submission**, not about creating buttons specifically. The behavior provides the **submission capability** of a submit button (implicit submission, activation handling, default role, etc.). A custom element using this behavior doesn't *have* to look or act like a `<button>` as it just gains the ability to submit forms via click/keyboard and participate in implicit form submission.

For the "what other behaviors might we need" question, the Future work section lists generic button behavior (for popover invocation, commands), reset buttons, inputs (text entry, validation, selection APIs), labels (for/label association and focus delegation), forms, radio groups, and tables.

A few thoughts on the subclassing suggestion:

1. Buttons might be a good candidate (no UA shadow DOM), but other elements like `<input>` (has UA shadow DOM for date pickers, sliders) or `<select>` would each need their own analysis. This might not be a general solution.
2. As you mention, composability isn't directly possible.
3. Even if we solve the `is=` and Shadow DOM/ElementInternals issues, I'm not sure this addresses WebKit's concern that customized built-ins are "logically different from the element they extend" which affects accessibility semantics. But I could be wrong about that.

---

@kyubisation, thank you for your API suggestions. I'll incorporate them in the next update to the explainer.

While an interface like `internals.disabled`, `internals.focusable`, `internals.checked`, etc. looks straightforward, each of these primitives carries semantic and accessibility implications that interact with each other. This is also why `popovertarget` is limited to buttons (originally intended for any element, but the accessibility requirements around focusability and activation made buttons the practical choice). These interdependencies are why we're proposing (submitting) behaviors rather than individual flags.

Yes, I am fully aware (as I have been following this discussion for years now).

Again, this is my personal opinion, with my focus being on having access to similar capabilities as native elements do
As mentioned, I see no clear benefits to gating these APIs behind behaviors. Simple properties on ElementInternals should allow for easier use and more flexibility.
(While maybe not the best example, currently something like this is possible for `:disabled` and the aria disabled state, which can be achieved via `formAssociated = true` and adding the `disabled` attribute.)

If properties on ElementInternals are rejected as an option, I would argue for separated, distinct behaviors (e.g. DisabledBehavior, CheckedBehavior, PopoverBehavior, etc.) in addition to the aggregated, full functionality behaviors.
Updated the explainer with a new API shape that gets rid of `behaviorsList` and makes the behaviors array unmutable (among a few other *minor* changes). Please take another look if you're interested!

@anaskim this is looking really good. Some notes:

- Can you help me understand how the order would enforce precedence? Especially with the designed userland calling convention it seems like precedence would be arbitrary. I think arbitrary is fine for userland but of course we'd need to specify exactly the interplay of built-ins. In Gecko at least we have a flag to say that an event has been handled (in addition to defaultPrevented) and so we could execute all behaviours click handlers, but the first one to handle it would cause others to skip. Enforcing an order of precedence _might_ preclude some novel interplay; worth figuring out if arbitrary order vs enforced causes more problems than it solves.

- Your "Use case: Design system button" sketch doesn't handle attribute changes, it would be interesting to go through the motions and sketch that. Right now the fact that `.behaviors` is an immutable array means the design system button diverges from platform's button in that `type=` can only set the behaviour once. This maybe speaks to the first point around order of precedence; perhaps a button loading all 3 behaviours at once is okay?

- The sketch for `PlatformBehavior` mentions `behaviorAttachedCallback` and `behaviorDetatchedCallback` but later on a sketch hints at `setDefaultRole`, it might be worth enumerating what else `PlatformBehavior` would need to ship with in order to explain `HTMLButtonBehavior`. Perhaps it's worth writing a sketch for a userland implementation of `HTMLButtonBehavior`, because I imagine it might help discover and/or settle any ambiguities of semantics.

- Further to that; I guess userland will want to monitor attribute changes. It would be unfortunate to have to rely on MutationObservers for this.

- I have a slight preference to avoid the word `behavior`, a lot of the web is written in American English and it's unavoidable to hit some instances on divergent spelling, aside from that though the word `behavior` is a bit of a chore to type so if we could find a shorter/easier-to-spell word that would be _nice_.

@keithamus Thank you for the feedback! The explainer has been updated to address your points.

---
> Can you help me understand how the order would enforce precedence? [...] In Gecko at least we have a flag to say that an event has been handled (in addition to defaultPrevented) and so we could execute all behaviours click handlers, but the first one to handle it would cause others to skip.

Chromium has the same pattern — `Event::DefaultHandled()` / `Event::SetDefaultHandled()`, separate from `defaultPrevented`. 

Whether you iterate forward (handled-flag) or reverse (last-in-wins), each behavior gets a chance to handle the event and can decline (e.g., it's disabled or doesn't have a form). Web authors control priority by choosing array position.

---
> Your "Use case: Design system button" sketch doesn't handle attribute changes [...] perhaps a button loading all 3 behaviours at once is okay?

Good question. The explainer now includes a [section on dynamically changing the type attribute](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#dynamically-changing-the-type-attribute) explaining why loading all three behaviors simultaneously doesn't work:

- `disabled` is user-facing, and doesn't scope behaviors. Under last-in-wins, only the last behavior's `disabled` value determines the element's state, so toggling non-active behaviors' `disabled` has no effect on which behavior responds.
- `name`/`value` from the last behavior win, so the submit behavior's name/value might be overwritten by the last behavior listed.
- Under strict last-in-wins, only the last behavior's handler runs (element can never submit). Under additive events, all handlers run (element submits and resets)

The recommended pattern is single behavior determined at connection time. The full `attributeChangedCallback` handling for `disabled`, `formaction`, etc. is now included in the example.

---
> It might be worth enumerating what else PlatformBehavior would need to ship with [...] Perhaps it's worth writing a sketch for a userland implementation of HTMLButtonBehavior

I've included the section [ElementBehavior API](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#elementbehavior-api) (previously `PlatformBehavior`) in Future work to list the elements that `ElementBehavior` would need to have (`element`, `setDefaultRole()`, `setDefaultTabIndex()`, and `behaviorAttachedCallback(internals)`) and a userland `HTMLButtonBehavior` implementation to exemplify the API.

---

> I guess userland will want to monitor attribute changes. It would be unfortunate to have to rely on MutationObservers for this.

I don't think MutationObservers are needed here since custom elements already receive synchronous attribute change notifications via `attributeChangedCallback`. Are you referring to a different scenario?

---
> I have a slight preference to avoid the word behavior [...] if we could find a shorter/easier-to-spell word that would be nice.

The explainer now includes a [naming alternatives open question](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#is-there-a-better-name-than-behavior-for-this-concept). I welcome your preference or suggestions.

@annevk, let me know if I missed anything or if you have more feedback on the proposal, happy to discuss further at the next WHATNOT.

Some feedback after discussing this with @annevk and @lukewarlow on WHATWG matrix:

1) I think that assigning a behavior at connection time based on an attribute is not a great pattern and doesn't add much on top of making it a static behavior like `formAssociated`. If it's attribute based it should be mutable, and if it's not it can be static. This proposal is a bit "neither here or there" in terms of mutability.

Duplicating the `type` based separation from `input` is an unnecessary complication and anyway doesn't work if it's immutable after setting. What is the advantage of `<my-input type=submit>` over  `<my-input-submit>`? If a library wants to expose it as a type attribute they can wrap an element with submit behavior inside their shadow root and compose things that way, controlling their own mutability by creating the inner element only at connection time or destroying/recreating it based on attribute changes.

If it's static, perhaps it can take more design aspects from `formAssociated` in the way that it works and represented in the API - as in a set of static definitions of the element (whether as separate boolean or a string set like `class`).

It can even be `static formAssociated = 'submit'` since submit behavior implies form-associated anyway and this would be web compatible with booleans.

2) I don't think it's necessary to expose the behaviors as IDL interfaces if they don't hold any state and might have special interactions with each other. Standard-defined strings (like input/script types and link rels) are first class citizens.

Thanks @noamr, @annevk, and @lukewarlow for the discussion on the WHATWG matrix. I updated the explainer with the following points to try to address your feedback.
 
 1. On the mutability framing: the set of behaviors attached to an element is static after `attachInternals()`. Attribute-driven selection of which behaviors to attach happens once, in `connectedCallback`, before the element is observable. The reason for that decision (rather than full runtime add/remove) is now documented in the section [Dynamic behaviors](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#dynamic-behaviors): form ownership transitions, role transitions observable to assistive technologies, focusability transitions, and in-flight activation (mousedown happened with the behavior attached, mouseup arrives after it was removed) all become observable to authors and bring up more complex cases. I also wrote a proposed path forward on this in [Alternative API design 3](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#alternative-api-design-3-behavior-scoped-behaviordisabled).
`<my-input type=submit>` vs `<my-input-submit>`: the advantage is the pattern major component libraries already ship today. [User research](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#user-research) walks through Shoelace, Material Web, Adobe Spectrum, and Fluent: all four expose a single class whose form activation is selected by the `type` attribute, with a hidden `<button type=submit>` proxy in the shadow root or a JS reimplementation of submission. The proposal exists to give them and the rest of custom elements authors a first-class alternative to that proxy. Splitting into `<my-input-submit>` / `<my-input-reset>` / `<my-input-button>` is the [Alternative 1 (mixins)](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#alternative-1-static-class-mixins) tradeoff: it requires more classes for a "single" element and loses the ability to swap behavior on a single rendered DOM node, which design systems rely on so they don't have to destroy/recreate the host element on attribute change (see [Use case: Design system button](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#use-case-design-system-button)).
"compose by wrapping a behavior-element inside the shadow root": that's the current workaround, and it's what those libraries do today. It makes labeling and accessibility delegation harder, and forces every library to invent its own destroy/recreate logic for attribute changes. Asking them to keep doing that is what the proposal is trying to move past.
`static formAssociated = 'submit'`: this is what the (new) [Alternative API design 2](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#alternative-api-design-2-static-behavior-list-on-the-class) currently captures. It has the following constraints: no per-instance configurable state and no attribute-driven selection of the active behavior.
 
 2. On IDL interfaces vs standard-defined strings: `HTMLSubmitButtonBehavior` is not stateless: it carries nine writable per-instance properties (`disabled`, `formAction`, `formEnctype`, `formMethod`, `formNoValidate`, `formTarget`, `name`, `value`, plus read-only `form` and `labels`), mirroring `HTMLButtonElement`. See [Accessing behavior state](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/PlatformProvidedBehaviors/explainer.md#accessing-behavior-state). The question is: do we need inheritance or composability? A lot of stuff in web components already eschews inheritance (for various reasons). E.g. FormData doesn't appear on a Custom Element just because it inherits something. You have to work to get it there. If platform behaviours can be split down into a (somewhat) coherent set of primitives, then even inheritance becomes largely "re-use this bag of behaviours", and incidentally can solve a lot of issues like "this link is actually a button". There's a great article by Ryan Fleury (of [RAD Debugger](https://github.com/EpicGames/raddebugger)) discussing issues coming up in UI design all the time, and how composability trumps "let's define a hierarchy of classes": https://www.dgtlgrove.com/p/ui-part-3-the-widget-building-language
The following list is pulled from a project I work on that has relatively complex user interface requirements. It is a set of possible “features” or “effects” that I can apply at each node in a widget hierarchy: - Clickability—taking mouse events and hovering, responding to clicks and drags - Mouse wheel scrolling to shift the “view offset” - Keyboard focusing behavior—another path for producing “clicks” or “presses” in a keyboard-driven fashion - Being, and appearing, disabled and non-interactive to the user - “Floating” on the X axis—skipping layout on this axis, effectively - “Floating” on the Y axis - Allowing overflow on the X axis—skipping size-constraint-solving on this axis - Allowing overflow on the Y axis - Requiring a drop shadow to be rendered - Requiring a background to be rendered - Requiring a border to be rendered - Requiring text to be rendered - Hot animation visualization - Active animation visualization - Arbitrary “render command buffer” attachment - Center-aligned text - Clipping rectangle for children widgets - The X-axis position being smoothly animated across frames - The Y-axis position being smoothly animated across frames - Bypassing text-truncation with ellips ... each “widget kind”—Button, Checkbox, Slider, whatever else we might need—is one particular feature combination, or a small set of them. So, if you imagine the gigantic set of over a million feature combinations, these “widget kinds” are more-or-less just “poking into” that set. They’re just picking one specific combination and saying “this is something special”. What you can hopefully realize is that each “widget kind” cross-cuts into the feature set with other “widget kinds”. All three of the above “widget kinds” require nearly identical codepaths for clicking and dragging. ... confront the combinatoric explosion of feature-combinations head-on. Instead, we can prepare up-front for 2^N possible feature combinations by implementing codepaths for only N features.

@dmitriid 

> The question is: do we need inheritance or composability?

Both! As I said in my comment:

> Combining inheritance AND traits is pretty common in OOP languages.

Some things are better suited to inheritance, others are better suited to composition.

In the case of a submit button, you also want all the `HTMLButtonElement` API that comes with it, and the only ways to get that are either inheritance or language-level composition (which we don't have yet).

A while back, I explored a Custom Elements version of Base UI, and this is the biggest (and only?) limitation I encountered.

In Base UI, components like `Menu.Trigger` and `Menu.LinkItem` render native `<button>` and `<a>` elements. With Custom Elements, there's no way to preserve that declarative API while inheriting the corresponding native behaviour.

The alternatives are undesirable: extra DOM wrappers, reimplementing native behaviour, or forcing consumers to author the underlying HTML elements themselves.

This is a fundamental obstacle to building high-quality, framework-independent UI libraries with Custom Elements.

I strongly agree with Lea that exploring native element inheritance for autonomous Custom Elements, rather than introducing a parallel behaviour system, is the way to go.
